## Background

Genomics is the study of an organism's complete genetic material, or genome. Rather than focusing on single genes, genomics investigates the functions and interactions of genes across the entire genome of an organism. Advances in sequencing technologies allow researchers to generate short or long DNA sequences called reads, which can be assembled to reconstruct longer genomic sequences. Following genome assembly, the resulting sequence can be compared with reference genome to identify similarities, differences and potentially important genomic features. Further, genome annotation is performed to identify genomic features and their functions. It includes structural annotation, which locates genes and other genomic components, as well as functional annotation, which assigns potential functions to existing genes by comparing them with information in known biological databases. These findings help researchers investigate the physiological functions of genes as well as identify metabolic pathways involved in biological processes, including production of metabolites that may potentially contribute to microbial interactions. In microorganisms such as yeasts, genome annotation can provide insights into the genetic basis of biological processes that may be associated with biocontrol activity. 
Microbial interactions play an important role in maintaining plant health as certain microorganisms can inhibit the growth of plant pathogens. In sustainable agricultural systems, biological control (biocontrol) uses beneficial organisms or their products to prevent or reduce plant diseases. This approach has gained substantial attention as a potential alternative to traditional chemical treatments. Among the microorganisms studied for biological control, yeasts have shown biocontrol potential through multiple mechanisms, including competition for nutrients and space, secretion of enzymes, toxin production and production of volatile organic compounds (VOCs). 
VOCs are small, volatile molecules with low water solubility and high vapor pressure. Examples include ethanol, 3-methyl-1-butanol and 2-phenylethanol (alcohols) as well as ethyl acetate and isoamyl acetate (esters). Yeast species can vary in these chemicals' relative quantity and composition. The production of VOCs in yeasts is associated with several metabolic pathways such as Ehrlich pathway and ester biosynthesis. These pathways involve specific enzymes that convert biochemical precursors such as metabolites into volatile organic compounds, such as alcohols and esters. Variations in genes encoding these enzymes may contribute to differences in VOC-producing potential among different yeast strains.
Previous studies have demonstrated the potential of Wickerhamomyces anomalus as a biocontrol agent through production of volatile organic compounds. For instance, studies have shown that this wild yeast isolate produces several VOCs, including those associated with inhibition of fungal infections and postharvest diseases. Ethyl acetate is one of the volatile compounds of interest because of its biocontrol potential. Similarly, Hanseniaspora uvarum has been studied for its capacity to generate volatile organic compounds that could be utilized in biological control. Past studies have recognized ethyl acetate produced by this as biocontrol agent for pathogen linked to rot in tomato fruits.
Although VOC synthesis and biocontrol potential have been observed in both yeast species, differences in genetic composition and metabolic capabilities may affect their ability to produce these compounds. Genome annotation and comparative genomic analysis can help identify genes and predict metabolic pathways corresponding to VOC synthesis. 
This project aims to compare the observed genes and metabolic pathways associated with VOC production in the wild yeast isolates Wickerhamomyces anomalus NK1 and Hanseniaspora uvarum AD. For instance, genes involved in ester biosynthesis or the Eat1 homologs responsible for ethyl acetate production. The comparison will help identify genomic differences that may contribute to variations in their potential for VOC-mediated biocontrol. 

## Methods

### Sequencing Data and Provenance

Genomic DNA was extracted from two wild yeast isolates: Wickerhamomyces anomalus NK1 and Hanseniaspora uvarum AD by college. Before sequencing, the isolated DNA was checked for quality and prepared for library prepration. This involves repairing DNA or attaching adapters that help DNA sequence interact with Oxford Nanopore sequencing system. The prepared DNA library is loaded onto a flow cell with nanopores embedded in its membrane. Next, the ONT sequencing system detects and records the changes in ionic current caused by DNA molecules passing through nanopores. These electrical signals are converted to nucleotide sequences by basecalling software to generate FASTQ files containing sequence reads and their respective quality scores. For this project, we were directly provided FASTQ files generated from Oxford Nanopore long-read sequencing in two separate years (2025 and 2026) for both yeast isolates. As a result, combined FASTQ files (WA_final.fastq and HU_final.fastq) were used to provide more sequencing data and greater genome coverage for further donwstream analyses.

### Quality Assessment and read filtering

The quality of Oxford Nanopore sequencing reads can vary, with read quality decreasing towards the end of individual reads. Therefore, assessing read quality before genome assembly and subsequent downstream analyses is an important step. Quality control was performed using Sequali (version 1.0.2), which was installed and executed in a dedicated Conda environment (sequali-env). The FASTQ files were provided as input to generate HTML reports containing sequencing statistics, including read length distribution, N50, mean read length, Q-scores and relative adapter contamination.

Following the quality assessment, Filtlong (v0.3.1) was used to filter the long sequencing reads. Filtlong was installed and implemented in separate Conda environment (filtong_env). The --keep_percent 75 parameter was used to retain the best 75 % of reads based on its quality and length ranking. The resulting filtered FASTQ files were reassessed using Sequali to inspect changes in sequencing quality as well as compare the data with the original FASTQ files. These filtered FASTQ files were used to construct genome assembly.

### Genome Assembly

Genome assembly is the process of aligning and merging millions of fragmented DNA reads to reconstruct continuous genome sequence. Flye (2.9.6-bi802), a de novo assembler was installed and implemented in new Conda environment (flye_env) to complete genome assembly. The --nano-raw parameter specified that the input reads are raw Oxford Nanopore sequencing reads, while --genome-size 12m tells estimated genome size of 12 million base pairs. Flye aims at locating overlaps, constructing genome graph, resolve genomic structures and generating contigs for subsequent analysis.

### Genome Polishing

The resulting contigs from genome assembly may contain errors due to imprecisions in long-read sequencing. Genome polishing involves comparing the original sequencing reads against the assembled contigs to identify and rectify potential errors in the consensus sequence. Two rounds of polishing were performed using Medaka (version 2.2.1) to correct potential errors in genome assemblies. Medaka was equipped and executed in a separate Conda environment (medaka_final). The first round of Medaka was performed on assembled FASTA files and corresponding sequencing reads. The second round of polishing was conducted over polished files from Medaka round 1 and respective sequencing reads to further refine the consensus sequence.

### Assembly Quality Assessment

Assembly quality was assessed with QUAST (version 5.3.0) i.e., Quality Assessment tool for Genome Assemblies. It generates assembly statistics such as N50, number of contigs, total assembly length and contig length distribution to evaluate resultant assembly. QUAST was used with reference sequence to compare flye assembly against reference sequence. 
Genome completeness was assessed using BUSCO (version 6.0.0_cv1) i.e., Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologs. The genome mode was set to auto-lineage-euk, which automatically selects the most appropriate lineage dataset for eukaryotic genomes. It generates reports with BUSCO score displaying complete, duplicated, fragmented or missing genes to provide an approximation of assembly completeness.

### Genome Annotation

Structural genome annotation was done using funannotate (version 1.8.15) via Docker (nextgenusfs/funannotate:v1.8.15). The required Docker image was pulled and saccharomycetes BUSCO database was installed before running funannotate workflow.The polished genome assemblies were processed using funannotate clean (remove ahort contigs), sort (arrange contigs by length) and mask (soft masking repetitive regions) commands. Gene prediction was executed using funannotate predict command. The parameter --busco_db saccharomycetes was used to support gene prediction
Functional annotation of predicted protein sequences will be performed using eggNOG-mapper, installed in a dedicated Conda environment (eggnog_env) with Python 3.10. The predicted protein FASTA files generated by Funannotate will be used as input. eggNOG-mapper will use DIAMOND for sequence similarity searches to assign functional annotations based on evolutionary relationships and orthologous groups. The analysis will be performed using eight CPUs. Functional annotation results will be generated in tabular and Excel formats, and annotations will also be incorporated into the corresponding GFF files using the --decorate_gff option.
